request: A story about a girl named Alice and her best friend Bob, who happens to be a cat.

first_draft.title: Alice, Bob and the Moon Button
first_draft.text:
Alice had lost a button, and it was not just any button. It was round and blue, shiny as a puddle under the streetlight, and it had popped off her winter coat that morning. She searched the hallway, the kitchen and the bottom of the laundry basket. Nothing.

On the windowsill sat Bob, her ginger cat with one white paw, as if he had dipped it in milk and forgotten the rest. His tail swished slow as a clock.

"Where would a button go?" Alice asked him. Bob yawned, showing his pink tongue, and jumped down with a soft thump.

They searched under the sofa first. There was a dust bunny, a green crayon and one very old pea, which Alice put back in the bowl at once. Bob pushed his nose into the gap and sneezed. "Achoo!" The crayon rolled away, and Alice giggled so hard she had to sit down on the rug.

Next, the toy box. Bob climbed right in, rummaged with one paw, and came out wearing a woolly hat that was not his. He looked very pleased with himself. "Not a button, Bob. A hat," Alice said, and she plopped it back in.

Alice sat on the bottom stair and thought hard. The button must have fallen somewhere near the front door. Bob trotted past the radiator, where the warm blankets lived in a wicker basket. He sniffed. He circled. He patted the pile with one white paw, then stared at it very still.

"Are you hiding something?" Alice asked.

Bob blinked his slow cat blink, then strolled to the door and sat there as if he had never been near the basket at all.

Alice lifted the top blanket. Something rolled out, bounced once on the floor, and spun to a stop by her toes. It was blue and shiny, shaped exactly like a moon.

"You sneaky cat," Alice said, but she was smiling. Bob began to purr, which might have meant sorry, or might have meant that blanket was the coziest bed in the whole house.

Alice held the button in her palm. It was warm from the blanket. She felt a little cross, because Bob had made her search for ages, and a little happy, because she had found it, and a little sorry for him, because he had clearly loved that blanket very much.

"Next time, tell me," she whispered. Bob gave one tiny meow, which was the nearest thing to a promise a cat could make.

Alice ran to show Mum, who promised they would sew the button on together after supper. Alice tucked it into her pocket, where it clinked against a marble.

Night came softly. The streetlight glowed through the curtains, and the wind had gone quiet. Alice climbed into bed and pulled the duvet up to her chin. Bob hopped up beside her and turned in a circle, once, twice, three times, until he made a warm hollow against her feet.

The fridge hummed. The clock ticked, slow and low. The moon button sat on the bedside table, catching a little light. Bob's purr grew softer and softer, like a kettle cooling down.

"Goodnight, Bob," Alice breathed.

Bob's purr answered, very quietly. Then the room was still.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Captain Leo and the Muddy Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo found the old map tucked inside a biscuit tin under his bed. It was yellow at the edges and smelled of dust and cinnamon. An X was drawn in red crayon beside the apple tree at the bottom of the garden.

"Rocket, we're going treasure hunting," Leo whispered.

Rocket, his scruffy brown dog, thumped his tail so hard that the bedroom lamp wobbled. Leo tucked the map into his pocket, grabbed his spade, and they tiptoed down the back steps into the cool evening air.

The garden was full of hiding places. Tall grass swished against their legs. A watering can clanged against the fence. Rocket sniffed at every bush as if it were the most exciting thing in the world. "Follow the map," Leo said, squinting at the wobbly lines. "Ten giant steps from the shed. Then turn toward the apple tree."

One giant step. Two giant steps. Rocket took three, because his legs were shorter, and he yipped with joy. At step ten, the ground went squelch under Leo's sneakers. Then Rocket began to dig. Dirt flew everywhere, like a brown snowstorm, and a clump landed right on Leo's nose.

"Rocket! Wait, we need to be careful!" Leo laughed, wiping his face. He knelt down and scraped gently with his spade. Clink. Something hard touched the metal. Leo's heart drummed like a rainstorm on a tin roof.

He pulled out a small wooden box, damp and muddy. Rocket sat back on his haunches, ears up, tail sweeping the grass. Leo brushed off the lid and lifted it slowly.

Inside, nestled on a folded scrap of paper, was a shiny gold coin with a crooked smile stamped on it. Beneath it lay a note in careful handwriting: For the finder, a pirate's thanks. Leo gasped. Rocket barked once, very loudly, and then yawned a huge yawn that made Leo giggle.

Leo held the coin up to the porch light. It winked at him. "Captain Rocket," he said solemnly, "we have found our treasure."

The back door creaked open. Mum's voice floated across the garden. "Leo? Rocket? It's time for bed, you two."

Leo tucked the coin safely in his pocket and the wooden box under his arm. Rocket trotted beside him, his paws quiet on the cool grass. The sky above was turning the deep blue of a calm sea. A single star blinked on, then another.

Back in his room, Leo placed the box on his shelf, next to his best pirate hat. He pulled up his blanket. Rocket curled into a warm, fuzzy circle at the foot of the bed.

The lamp glowed soft and low. The map rested on the pillow beside Leo's head. Outside, the apple tree rustled gently in the breeze, and the garden settled into sleep.

Goodnight, Captain Leo. Goodnight, Rocket.

first_draft.title: Pip and the Wobbly Wings
first_draft.text:
High on a rocky hill lived a little dragon named Pip. Pip had green scales, a wiggly tail, and two small wings that looked like wet leaves.

Every morning the big dragons zoomed past the clouds. Whoosh! Swoosh! Whoomph! They looped and dipped and rolled in the sky.

Pip stood at the edge of the hill and watched. Her tummy went flip, flop, flip.

"Today is the day," said Mama Dragon. "Jump, and spread your wings."

Pip jumped. Her wings flapped. Thup, thup, thup. Then she tumbled down into the soft grass with a plop.

"Ouch," said Pip. "Not yet."

The next morning, Pip tried again. She hopped. She flapped. She wobbled and bumped into a bush. Rustle, rustle, scratch.

A field mouse peeked out. "Why are you so wobbly?" it squeaked.

"My wings are scared," said Pip. "And so am I."

The mouse scratched its ear. "Hmm. Maybe your wings need a little practice, like my tiny feet on the tall grass."

So Pip and the mouse practiced together. They played a game called Leaf Catch. Pip flapped low over the grass. The mouse zig-zagged and squeaked, "Eek! Over here!"

Pip giggled so hard that she hiccupped. Hic! Hic! A puff of sparkly smoke floated up, and it smelled like warm cinnamon.

Then Pip noticed something. When she was laughing, her wings were loose and floppy. They felt light, like a dandelion seed.

"Let's try that again," Pip whispered. She thought of the silly mouse and the tickly grass. She hopped. She wiggled. She let her wings go soft.

Whoosh! The wind lifted her up, up, up. Her wings went flap, flap, glide.

"I'm flying!" Pip sang. She looped over the hill and waved at the cows below.

When she landed, Mama Dragon was smiling. Pip's tail swished with happiness.

That night, the moon rose soft and round. Pip curled up in her warm nest of moss. The wind hummed a slow, sleepy song. Hoo-oo. Hoo-oo.

Pip's wings folded close, like a blanket. Her eyes grew heavy.

The mouse yawned in the grass. The stars blinked, one by one.

Good night, little dragon. Shh. Sleep now.

final.title: Pip and the Wobbly Wings
final.text:
High on a rocky hill lived a little dragon named Pip. Pip had green scales, a wiggly tail, and two small wings that looked like wet leaves.

Every morning the big dragons zoomed past the clouds. Whoosh! Swoosh! Whoomph! They looped and dipped and rolled in the sky. Their wings sounded like flags in a windy field.

Pip stood at the edge of the hill and watched. Her tummy went flip, flop, flip. Her toes curled tight around a pebble.

"Today is the day," said Mama Dragon. "Jump, and spread your wings."

Pip jumped. Her wings flapped. Thup, thup, thup. Then she tumbled down into the soft grass with a plop.

"Ouch," said Pip, rubbing her nose. "Not yet."

The next morning, Pip tried again. She hopped. She flapped. She wobbled and bumped into a bush. Rustle, rustle, scratch. A cloud of dandelion fluff puffed up and tickled her eyes.

A field mouse peeked out from under a leaf. "Why are you so wobbly?" it squeaked.

"My wings are scared," said Pip. "And so am I."

The mouse scratched its ear. "Hmm. Maybe your wings need a little practice, like my tiny feet on the tall grass. My name is Tilly, by the way."

"I'm Pip," said the dragon, and her tail gave a small, shy wiggle.

So Pip and Tilly practiced together. They played a game called Leaf Catch. Pip flapped low over the grass. Tilly zig-zagged and squeaked, "Eek! Over here!" Pip swooped left. Pip swooped right. Whoops! She flopped right on top of Tilly's leaf.

Pip giggled so hard that she hiccupped. Hic! Hic! A puff of sparkly smoke floated up, and it smelled like warm cinnamon. Tilly giggled too, and her whiskers wiggled like jelly.

Then Pip noticed something. When she was laughing, her wings were loose and floppy. They felt light, like a dandelion seed.

"Let's try that again," Pip whispered. She thought of the silly mouse and the tickly grass. She hopped. She wiggled. She let her wings go soft, the way a noodle goes soft in warm soup.

Whoosh! The wind lifted her up, up, up. Her wings went flap, flap, glide. Her belly tickled as the hill grew small below her.

"I'm flying!" Pip sang. She looped over the hill and waved at the cows below. Moo, said the cows. Moo, moo.

When she landed, Mama Dragon was smiling. Pip's tail swished with happiness, swish, swish, swish.

That night, the moon rose soft and round. Pip curled up in her warm nest of moss, next to her new friend's little burrow. The wind hummed a slow, sleepy song. Hoo-oo. Hoo-oo.

Pip's wings folded close, like a blanket. Her eyes grew heavy.

The mouse yawned in the grass. The stars blinked, one by one.

Good night, little dragon. Shh. Sleep now.

At midnight, when the kitchen clock went tick, tock, tock, the fridge door creaked open just a crack. Cold white light spilled onto the tiles like spilled milk. Inside, something giggled.

Juniper crept downstairs in her striped socks, her teddy tucked under one arm. She peeked around the doorframe. There, on the top shelf, a row of carrots was doing the cha-cha.

"One, two, crunch-a-munch!" sang a sprightly carrot named Pip, hopping onto a butter dish. Beside him, a lumpy potato rolled in a slow, wobbly waltz. A stalk of broccoli wore a paper hat that said PARTY, and it was slightly too big.

"Oh no," whispered Juniper. "The party has started without a host!"

The problem was the cheese. Its wedge sat in the middle of the shelf, pale and sulky, with its crumbs flaking off. "Nobody invited me," it sniffled. "I'm too smelly for dancing."

Juniper tapped her chin. Smelly cheese needed something sweet to cheer it up. But the fridge was full, and the cupboard was far away, and the party was getting louder. Pip began to spin in circles. A pea rolled off the shelf and went pitter-patter across the floor.

"Shh, shh!" hissed a leek from the back. "If Mum wakes up, we'll be pickled!"

Juniper had an idea. She fetched the jar of honey from the counter, and a small bunch of grapes from the bowl. Then she knelt by the fridge and held them out, very politely.

"Excuse me," she said. "I think this party needs a guest of honour. Would you like to dance with me?"

The cheese blinked. Slowly, it sat up. A little crumb fell off like a shy smile. Juniper drizzled a golden drop of honey across its rind, and the cheese gave a happy, squeaky hum.

"Oh! Oh my!" cried Pip. "Now everyone can dance!"

So they did. The carrots cha-cha-ed. The potato waltzed. The broccoli bopped in its too-big hat, and the pea rolled a neat loop around Juniper's toes. Juniper hummed along, tapping her socks on the cold tiles, while the grapes bounced like tiny drums.

But the dancing grew wild, and a tomato went rolling toward the edge of the shelf. Juniper gasped and cupped her hands just in time. The tomato landed with a soft plop. "Thank you," it said, a bit breathless. "That was close."

At last, the music slowed. Pip yawned a big orange yawn. The potato drooped against a jar of pickles. The broccoli's hat slid down over one eye, and the cheese, now warm and cheerful, sighed a long, sleepy sigh.

Juniper gathered the vegetables in a gentle heap. "Time for bed," she whispered. "Lights off. Doors closed. Party over."

One by one, the fridge light dimmed. The carrots curled into a tidy row. The pea tucked itself into the crisper drawer. Somewhere, a sleepy leek murmured, "Same time tomorrow?"

Juniper pressed the fridge door softly shut, and the kitchen went quiet. The clock ticked slowly. Tock. Tock. Tock.

Upstairs, under her warm blanket, Juniper snuggled close to her teddy. Her eyelids grew heavy, and the sounds of the house settled into a hush.

Goodnight, little carrots. Goodnight, sleepy cheese. Goodnight, quiet kitchen, and goodnight, Juniper.

first_draft.title: Juniper, Biscuit, and the Thimble Cat
first_draft.text:
The moon had a crooked grin tonight, and Juniper could see it through her window like a silver spoon dipped in milk.

Juniper was seven, and she had a teddy bear named Biscuit who smelled of lavender and old pancakes. Biscuit had a loose button on one paw, and Juniper had promised to fix it before bedtime. But when she looked under her pillow, the sewing kit was gone.

"Biscuit, where did it go?" she whispered.

From the hallway came a soft clink, clink, clink. Juniper tiptoed out in her socks. The floorboards creaked, eek, eek, like a mouse with a squeaky shoe.

At the top of the stairs sat Mr. Pilchard, the round grey cat from next door, who sometimes visited through the cat flap. He had a thimble balanced on his nose and the sewing kit tucked under one fat paw.

"Mr. Pilchard, that's mine!" Juniper said, trying not to giggle. The cat blinked slowly, as if he had every right in the world. Then he sneezed, and the thimble went flying down the stairs. Ding! Ding! Ding! It bounced all the way to the bottom.

Juniper laughed so hard she had to sit down on the top step. Mr. Pilchard looked very pleased with himself.

"Okay," she said. "You can help me find the thimble, and then I'll get my button fixed. Deal?"

Mr. Pilchard gave a small, grumbly purr, which Juniper decided meant yes.

They crept down together. Juniper peered under the sofa, where she found two gold coins, a lost sock, and a crumb shaped like a star. Mr. Pilchard sniffed behind the umbrella stand. He pawed at the velvet curtain until it swayed. Then he stopped and stared at the thimble, which had rolled neatly into the empty fruit bowl.

"Clever cat," Juniper whispered.

Back upstairs, she sat on her bed with Biscuit on her lap. She threaded the needle, though her fingers wobbled. Stitch, pull. Stitch, pull. The little button grew snug again, like a tooth that had found its home.

"There," she said. "Good as new."

Mr. Pilchard curled up at the foot of the bed, a warm grey loaf with his tail tucked over his nose. Juniper tucked Biscuit under her chin. The room was hushed, and the moon's crooked grin had softened into a smile.

Outside, the wind hummed a low, slow song through the apple tree. Branches swayed. Leaves whispered. Somewhere a owl said hoo, and then said hoo again, more quietly.

Juniper's eyes grew heavy. Her breath slowed, in and out, soft as a feather.

Goodnight, Biscuit, she thought. Goodnight, Mr. Pilchard. Goodnight, moon.

The room grew still, and the stars kept watch.

first_draft.title: Minnow and the Sock-Loving Monster
first_draft.text:
Every morning, Minnow found fewer socks in the laundry basket. A red one vanished on Monday. A striped one went on Tuesday. On Wednesday, a yellow sock with a hole in its heel disappeared without a trace.

"Something is eating them," said Grandpa Olu, rubbing his whiskery chin. "I'd say it's a monster with a very sock-shaped appetite."

Minnow did not believe in monsters. Not really. But on Thursday night, when the house was quiet and the clock ticked slowly on the wall, she heard a noise from under the stairs. Crunch. Munch. Slurp. Then a small, surprised burp.

She crept down in her pyjamas, flashlight clutched tight, and shone it into the dark cupboard. Two round yellow eyes blinked back at her.

The monster was no bigger than a laundry basket. Its fur was the colour of wet moss, its ears stuck up like teapot handles, and its mouth was stuffed full of woolly sock. Sock number four, Minnow thought, which was very annoying.

"Hello," whispered Minnow. "Are you the one who's been eating our socks?"

The monster swallowed with a loud gulp. "I'm Gobblewick," he said politely. "Only the odd ones. Odd socks taste the best. Stripy ones are my favourite. Yellow ones are a bit tickly."

Minnow thought hard. Monsters, she knew, liked food. She tiptoed to the kitchen and came back with a pancake from the plate Grandpa had left on the counter, still steaming, with a drizzle of syrup on top.

"Try this," she said.

Gobblewick snatched it, chewed with his eyes closed, and sighed. "Oh, that's lovely. Sticky and warm. But socks are warmer." Then he picked up a green one and munched it anyway.

Minnow tried again. She fetched a clothes peg and clipped the laundry basket shut. Gobblewick looked at the peg. He looked at the basket. Then, very neatly, he unclipped it with one long purple tongue. "Pop!" went the peg across the room.

Minnow sat down on the cold floor and watched him. That was when she noticed his feet. They poked out from under the stairs, all six of them, and the tips were wiggling and blue.

"Gobblewick," she said slowly, "are your toes cold?"

The monster's ears drooped. He pulled a heap of odd socks closer around himself, a nest of stripes and spots and woolly lumps. "Always," he admitted. "The cupboard is draughty. Socks are the only warm things I've ever found."

Minnow ran upstairs for her old fleece blanket, the one with the bears on it, and came back with it trailing behind her like a cape. She tucked it round his shoulders. Gobblewick wriggled until he was cosy, then let out a long, happy sigh that rattled the coats on their hooks.

"Now," said Minnow, "I think you have some socks to give back."

Gobblewick looked guilty. But he dug into his nest and handed them over, one by one: the red one, the striped one, and at the very bottom, the yellow one with the hole in its heel. "That one was the most fun to chew," he said quietly.

The next morning, the laundry basket was full. Every sock was there, in pairs, ready for school. Grandpa found a fresh stack of pancakes waiting on the counter, with a note in Minnow's careful writing: For the cupboard, please.

That night, when the house had gone quiet and the clock ticked slower than before, Minnow pulled her quilt up to her chin. Under the stairs, a soft rumble rolled through the wall, like a sleepy tide going out.

"Night, Gobblewick," she whispered.

From the dark came one slow, sleepy word. "Mmm... night."
notes: The monster now only nibbles socks and pancakes, never people, so it stays friendly and harmless.

Eeek. Creeeak. Crrrunch. Then, from somewhere beneath the floorboards, came a long, wobbly moan. "Ooooooh... ooooooh..."

Wren pulled her quilt up to her nose. In the bunk below, her cousin Mateo snored like a tiny tugboat chugging up a river.

"Mateo," she whispered. "Mateo, are you awake?"

"Hrrmph," said Mateo, and rolled over.

first_draft.title: The Bell for Two
first_draft.text:
Dame Imogen clanked across the orchard, clink, clank, clonk, with every step. Her helmet was a size too big, and it wobbled like a jelly on a plate.

"Today," she told the apple trees, "I shall ring the evening bell of Mossgrove Castle!"

The apple trees rustled politely. Somewhere behind the wall, a goose honked.

Every evening, the bell was rung by whichever knight reached the tower first. That was usually Sir Anouk, who had legs as long as a heron's and had never once tripped over his own sword. But today Imogen had a plan. She would beat him in a duel, and the bell would be hers.

Sir Anouk strolled through the orchard gate, swinging his wooden sword. Whoosh! Whoosh! "En garde, Imogen!"

"En garde!" cried Imogen, and she lifted her sword high above her head. It was much heavier than it looked. It slipped from her fingers, sailed over the wall, and landed with a splash in the duck pond.

"Oh," said Imogen.

Quack, said the ducks.

Sir Anouk laughed so hard he had to sit down on a pumpkin. "Do you surrender?"

"Certainly not!" Imogen marched to the hedge and snapped off a long, bendy stick. "Now it is a stick duel!"

They circled each other on the squelchy grass. Clonk, squeak, went Imogen's armour. Whack, went Anouk's stick against her shoulder plate. Bong! went the metal, and the sound rolled across the orchard like a giant clearing his throat.

Imogen swung back with a mighty whoosh. Her stick missed Anouk by a whisker, flew around in a wide loop, and wrapped itself neatly around his cape. Anouk spun round and round like a spinning top.

"Help!" he giggled. "I am a very dizzy knight!"

Imogen tugged at the stick, but her helmet slid down over her eyes. Now she could see nothing but a small square of blue sky and the tip of her own nose.

"Where are you?" she called, waving her arms.

"Here!" said Anouk, who had somehow ended up tangled in the apple tree. A plump apple dropped from a branch and landed on his helmet. Bonk.

Imogen giggled so hard that her helmet popped right off. It rolled down the path like a runaway cooking pot, all the way to the gate, and stopped at the feet of a very surprised hen.

When they had both untangled themselves, they sat side by side in the warm grass, rubbing their elbows and laughing. Anouk picked a leaf out of his hair.

"We both want the bell," he said.

Imogen looked up at the tall tower. Its bell rope hung down beside the great wooden door, swaying gently in the breeze. It was a long rope, and a very heavy bell.

"I think," said Imogen slowly, "that the bell is big enough for two."

Anouk grinned. "Shall we ring it together?"

So they walked to the tower, side by side, with Imogen's helmet tucked under one arm and Anouk's cape dragging behind him. They each took hold of the rope. They counted together. "One... two... three!"

Bim-bom! The bell sang out across the fields. Birds lifted from the hedges. The ducks quacked, the goose honked, and the hen clucked in surprise. In the windows of the village, people waved and smiled.

Now the sun was sinking low, painting the castle walls a soft gold. The bell hummed one last time and then grew quiet.

Imogen's armour gave one final, tired clink. Sir Anouk gave a long, slow yawn. They walked home through the orchard, very slowly, past the pond where the wooden sword floated like a sleepy little boat.

The ducks tucked their heads beneath their wings. The apples hung still on their branches. The stars came out, one by one, like tiny lamps being lit.

Imogen climbed into bed, and her helmet sat on the pillow beside her, like a friendly moon.

"Goodnight, Anouk," she whispered.

Far away, the bell gave a soft, sleepy hum.

Goodnight.

request: Maya is starting at a new school on Monday and she's nervous about making friends

first_draft.title: Maya and the Clicking Marbles
first_draft.text:
Maya sat on her bed on Sunday night. Her new school shoes waited by the door, shiny and stiff. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow was a brand-new school.

"What if nobody wants to play with me?" she whispered.

Her teddy, Biscuit, stared back with button eyes. Biscuit never had answers.

Mum came in smelling of lemon soap. She sat down on the blanket. "New schools feel big," she said. "Even for grown-ups. Would you like to pack something special?"

Maya thought hard. Then she chose a small glass jar of marbles. Inside, they clinked together. Click, clack, click. She tucked the jar into her bag, right next to her apple.

On Monday, the classroom smelled of crayons and wet paint. Twenty children chattered like noisy starlings. Maya stood by the door, gripping her bag straps. Her tummy went flip, flop, flip.

"Hello," said a voice. A boy with spiky hair waved a crayon. "I'm Hector. You can sit here."

Maya sat down. She peeked at his drawing. A dragon with seven legs galloped across the page.

"That dragon has too many legs," Maya said. Then her cheeks went hot.

Hector frowned, then grinned. "It needs seven! One for each sock. Otherwise it gets too wobbly."

Maya giggled. "Dragons don't wear socks!"

"They have very cold feet," Hector said seriously, and he wiggled his toes under the table. Maya laughed so loudly that the girl across the room turned around.

At playtime, the playground roared with shouting. Maya stood by the fence, holding her jar. Click, clack, click. Her heart felt small.

Then she spotted a girl named Edith, sitting alone under the big tree. Edith was drawing clouds. Nobody sat with her.

Maya took a deep breath. She walked over. "Would you like to help me count my marbles?"

Edith looked up slowly. "Okay," she whispered.

Maya tipped the jar. Marbles spilled onto the grass. Roll, roll, roll! They rolled in every direction.

"Got one!" shouted Hector, racing over with his dragon still in his hand.

"Got two!" called a girl named Priya, crawling under the bench.

Soon five children were on their knees in the grass. Edith found three marbles hiding under a leaf. Maya counted them all. Twenty-three, every one.

When the bell rang, Maya walked out with her jar in her arms. Edith was smiling. Hector waved his dragon. Priya said, "See you tomorrow, marble girl!"

That night, Mum asked, "How was your first day?"

Maya thought about it. "I have a dragon with seven socks," she said. "And a cloud artist. And a fast counter."

Mum laughed softly. "Sounds like a very good day."

Maya climbed into bed. The jar sat on her windowsill, catching the moonlight. Click. Clack. Click. Slower now.

Biscuit was tucked under her chin. The street outside went quiet. A car hummed far away, then faded.

Her eyes grew heavy. Her breathing slowed, soft as a feather.

Goodnight, marbles. Goodnight, dragon. Goodnight, Maya.

Shh.

request: Our old dog Biscuit died last week and Sam misses him a lot

first_draft.title: Biscuit's Blue Ball
first_draft.text:
The house had gone quiet in a way Sam had never heard before. At breakfast, no claws clicked across the kitchen floor. No warm nose nudged his knee under the table. At bedtime, the hallway stayed still, when it used to jingle with Biscuit's tags.

Biscuit had died last week. He had been old, with a grey muzzle and creaky legs, and he had spent his last summer lying in the patch of sunshine by the back door. Sam still missed him in small ways, like the gap in his mouth where a tooth used to be, which his tongue kept finding.

On Saturday, Mum said that some people like to keep a box of special things, so they can remember. Sam nodded. He wanted that very much. He went hunting for Biscuit's treasures: the red collar, the soft brush, and the squeaky blue ball.

The collar hung on its hook by the door. The brush was in the cupboard under the stairs. But the blue ball was nowhere at all.

Sam searched under the sofa, where dust bunnies rolled like tiny grey mice. He checked behind the bins and inside the wellies. He pulled out the washing basket and sneezed twice, achoo, achoo, right into a sock.

"Have you tried the garden?" called Mum from the kitchen, where the kettle was starting to whistle.

Sam pulled on his wellies, which squelched, and ran outside. The grass was cold and wet. He stood by the apple tree, where Biscuit always carried his ball, dropped it at Sam's feet, and then sat with his chin on his paws, watching the birds.

Sam looked up into the branches. He looked under the bench. Nothing. Then he remembered how Biscuit used to snuffle, nose down, through the low leaves. So Sam knelt, then lay on his tummy, and pushed his face close to the ground.

There, half hidden under a pile of brown leaves, was something blue. He wriggled his hand in and pulled it out. The ball gave a small, wobbly squeak, as if it had been waiting for him.

Sam held it tight and ran back inside. Mum was at the door, and her face went soft when she saw what he was holding.

"Looks like Biscuit was hiding it," she said gently. "Shall we make the box together?"

They sat on the kitchen floor with an empty shoebox, a pile of old photos, the collar, the brush, and the blue ball. Sam told stories. Biscuit had stolen a sausage right off a plate. Biscuit had chased his own tail until he fell over and looked very surprised about it. Mum laughed so hard she had to wipe her eyes.

Then Sam's voice wobbled. Mum put her arm around him. "I miss him too," she said.

Sam laughed, and then his throat went tight, and then he laughed again. Mum did not hurry him.

That night, the box sat on Sam's shelf, with the red collar hanging just above it. Sam held the blue ball in bed and pressed it softly now and then, so it gave one small squeak.

The fridge hummed downstairs. Outside, the apple tree rustled its last leaves. Sam's eyes grew heavy, and the room grew soft and dim.

"Goodnight, Biscuit," he whispered. The house was still quiet, but it was a gentle kind of quiet now.

first_draft.title: Thaddeus and the Creaky Branch
first_draft.text:
Far up in an old oak tree, an owl named Thaddeus gave a yawn so wide his feathers ruffled. "Hoo-oo," he sighed. "I am very, very sleepy."

He tucked his head under one wing and closed his big round eyes. Then, from the branch beside him, came a sound. Creak. Creak. Creak.

"Hush now," whispered Thaddeus. "Hush now, branch. I only want to rest."

But the branch only rocked in the breeze. Creak. Creak.

Thaddeus shuffled to the left. Creak. He shuffled to the right. Creak, creak. He sighed a small owl sigh and fluttered down to the old stump beside the pond.

The moss on the stump was soft and green. Thaddeus fluffed his feathers and settled in. Ribbit! Ribbit! A frog sat on a lily pad, singing as loud as he could.

"Hoo-oo, friend frog," said Thaddeus. "Could you sing a little more softly?"

The frog blinked his golden eyes. "Oh! Sorry, sorry," he croaked. He hopped away, singing tiny little ribbits.

But the wind still wobbled the branch above, and Thaddeus could not settle.

Just then, a small field mouse named Linnea popped out of the grass. Her whiskers twitched. "Hoo-oo," she said, "your tree is making a fuss. Shall I take a look?"

Thaddeus flew back to the oak, and Linnea scampered up the bark beside him. She peeked around the branch. "Aha!" she squeaked. "This branch rubs against the trunk. That is your creak."

Linnea tugged a tuft of soft moss from the stump. She tucked it snug between the branch and the trunk and pressed it down with her tiny paws.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Humming Blue Crystal
first_draft.text:
Zoe had a tortoise named Pebble, a windowsill full of crystals, and a secret wish to find something truly amazing. So on the first warm Saturday of spring, she tucked a lantern under one arm, cradled Pebble in both hands, and followed her dad up the grassy hill behind their cottage.

"Stay where I can see your light," said Dad, when they reached a dark gap in the hillside. A cool breeze drifted out. It smelled of rain and old, quiet stone.

Zoe clicked on the lantern. The walls sparkled back at her like frost on a window. Plink, plunk, went the drips from the ceiling. Pebble stepped in after her, slow and steady, one wrinkled foot at a time.

"Shhh," whispered Zoe. "Listen. Plink. Plunk. Plink."

They crept past shelves of pale rock and pools as clear as glass. The tunnel bent left, then right, then opened into a round room so bright that Zoe had to blink.

Purple crystals grew from every wall, some as tall as her arm, all shimmering like a thousand tiny stars. In the middle of the floor stood one enormous crystal, glowing a deep, sleepy blue.

"Oh," breathed Zoe. "Pebble, it's the most amazing thing I've ever seen." Pebble blinked his slow, golden eyes, as if he agreed.

Zoe pressed her palm against the blue crystal. It felt cool and smooth, and it hummed so softly she could feel it in her teeth. Then she noticed its base was wedged tight in a crack in the floor. It was stuck fast.

"Come on, you," she grunted, tugging with both hands. Her sneakers skidded on the damp stone. The crystal did not move one bit. She wiggled it. She tapped it with the lantern handle, which made a loud plonk and an echo that rolled around the room like a drum. Pebble stretched his neck and peered at the crack.

"It's not fair," Zoe said, sitting back on her heels. "I want to take it home and show everyone at school. Why won't you come out?"

Just then, something clinked against her knee. A small pink crystal, no bigger than a plum stone, had tumbled loose from a ledge. Zoe picked it up. Rainbow sparks danced across her palm when she tilted it toward the light.

Zoe looked around the room again, slowly this time. The big blue crystal was not alone. Every purple crystal on the wall was humming too, giving off a gentle glow, like a row of sleepy lamps.

"Dad!" she called. "Can you come and see?" His footsteps echoed down the tunnel, and his lantern bobbed closer. He crouched beside her, and his eyes went wide. "Well, look at this," he said softly.

Zoe explained about the stuck crystal. Dad nodded. "Those crystals grow only a tiny bit each year. Some of them have been growing longer than anyone has been alive. If we pulled that blue one out, the crack might split, the walls could shift, and this room would go dark forever."

Zoe's cheeks went hot. She had wanted the biggest, shiniest treasure, and now letting go felt heavy. She looked at Pebble, who had not hurried once since they arrived. He was simply enjoying the glow.

"Okay," she said at last. "We'll leave the blue one where it belongs. I'll keep the pink one, because it fell on its own."

Dad smiled. "That sounds wise. Some of the most wonderful things are best left where they are, so everyone can find them."

Zoe pulled out her notebook and sketched the room: the blue crystal, the purple walls, and Pebble in the corner. Dad held the lantern steady. They stayed quiet and listened to the drips, plink, plunk, until Zoe felt calm all the way down to her toes.

On the way out, Pebble led the way, his shell catching the last of the lantern light. Outside, the sun was low and golden, and the air smelled sweet with grass. Zoe understood something new. The most amazing treasures are not always the ones we carry home. Sometimes they are the ones we protect, and the careful, patient way, like Pebble's, is often the wisest way of all.

Back home, Zoe placed the pink crystal on the windowsill beside her others. Pebble tucked himself into his cozy box of straw. Dad switched off the big light and left only the soft lamp glowing.

The room grew quiet. Outside, the wind rested in the trees. Zoe's eyelids felt heavy, and her yawn was long and slow.

The pink crystal caught a sliver of moonlight and held it, very still.

"Goodnight, blue crystal," Zoe whispered. "Goodnight, purple lamps. Goodnight, Pebble."

Pebble sighed, and the room was still, and Zoe drifted softly into sleep.
